prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that renews lyric, essay and narrative through a formally inventive dialogue with classical antiquity, giving grief, desire and the act of translation new literary and material form

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading my colleagues. Carson has a voice I recognise at once and associate with this writer alone. Autobiography of Red reworks a Greek myth as a verse novel, and Nox makes elegy into a translated, archival and material object. In both, formal invention serves emotional and intellectual ends rather than ornament. The project has been sustained over several decades across verse narrative, lyric essay, drama and translation, and its central concerns (loss, desire, the inheritance of antiquity, the limits of translation) recur and deepen. That fits the criteria I treat as primary: distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, and imaginative and intellectual depth. All six openings place her first, but I do not treat that as evidence of merit. The case has to stand on the work, and I think it does. Cărtărescu and Zurita remain serious alternatives. Cărtărescu offers a visionary prose cosmos of great ambition, and Zurita a poetry of memorial scale and moral weight. For me the originality of Carson's formal solution is somewhat more settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of the achievement is hard to judge outside the original English page. It depends on typography, book design, allusion to Greek texts and object-like form. It is also open whether the scholar-poet hybrid is the right fit for Nobel's will and the 'ideal direction' criterion, and whether the weight of translation and classical scholarship inflates the case beyond her original writing. Her works are often short, fragmentary or occasional in scale, so the sustained breadth of the oeuvre needs more scrutiny than its fame suggests. If a close reading of the later books does not show real development rather than refinement of an established method, I would move toward Cărtărescu, whose large-scale ambition has clearly grown over time.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first for voice and form, but flags that the weight of her translations and classical scholarship relative to her original writing is a judgment call, and that her late work is less well known.
responses.response: I agree that the translations and scholarship should be secondary. The citation I propose rests on the original poetry, verse narrative and essays, with translation as context. On late work, I share the uncertainty and do not wish to claim more than public knowledge supports. I would only say that the question of sustained development is better tested by the sequence from Autobiography of Red to Nox and beyond than by any single book. If the committee cannot establish continuing invention in later work, that should count against her, and I would want it stated openly rather than assumed.

responses.point: Palm praises Carson's emotional exposure joined to classical learning, but notes that the work is often short or fragmentary in scale and that its sustained development into later work is the main thing to weigh.
responses.response: This is the point I find hardest to answer. Fragmentary scale is not a defect in itself, since compression is part of the method. But it does mean the case for sustained quality rests on consistency of invention across many small and medium forms rather than on a few monumental works, as it would for Cărtărescu. I would put it that way in committee. Where I differ slightly from Palm is in weighting: I read the repeated reinvention of the book as a form as evidence of development, not only of a stable manner.

responses.point: Sward sees Carson's intellectual depth and formal risk, but asks whether her heavy allusion to Greek texts makes her achievement partly scholarly, so that its weight as literature would need close reading.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and I do not think it can be dismissed. My view is that in the strongest books the learning is carried by voice and emotional structure, not displayed. Nox is the clearest example, since the philological apparatus is the vehicle of the elegy. But this is a claim about specific works that the committee must test by reading, not one to settle by reputation. I also note that Sward ranks Can Xue third where I ranked her eighth. My doubt is about whether a single uncompromising method renews itself across books, and about how much I can judge through translation. I would take her case seriously if colleagues who have read more of the translated corpus can show development.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first but notes that the range across genres and translations makes it hard to isolate the core of the achievement, and that assessment of the whole oeuvre rests on general public knowledge rather than a full reading.
responses.response: I share that caution and think it should shape the citation. I would isolate the core as the original poetry, verse narrative and essay in which the hybrid form is invented, and treat translations and stagings as context. The limit on our knowledge is real for every candidate on this list, not only Carson. That is a reason to be modest in how we phrase the citation, not a reason to prefer a candidate whose corpus we happen to know better. I would also accept Olsson's earlier point that the visual and book-object dimension should not be reduced to a text-only judgment.

uncertainties: How much of Carson's effect depends on typography, page design and Greek allusion, and whether that survives translation into Swedish and other languages.
Whether her later and more performance-based work shows real development, or refines an established method. My knowledge of it is uneven and not independently verified.
How the committee will weigh the hybrid scholar-poet mode against Nobel's will and the 'ideal direction' criterion.
Whether Cărtărescu's very large, dense Romanian prose is adequately represented in translation, and how his poetry and early work weigh against the major novels.
Whether Zurita's landscape and sky-writing works can be judged as literature through documentation alone, and how well his language holds up against the Spanish text.
statement.conflict_note: none apparent from the supplied profile
